Title or circuit: RCD protection for sockets and lighting
What it says: Socket-outlets rated up to 32 A on AC final circuits need additional protection from an RCD with a rated trip current of 30 mA or less. For one group of other locations the protection can be left out, but only after a documented risk assessment. In homes, AC final circuits that supply luminaires also need an RCD of 30 mA or less. Key rule: Socket-outlets up to 32 A, and household lighting circuits, need an RCD of 30 mA or less.

An arc fault detection device (AFDD) detects dangerous arcing in a final circuit. It is recommended on single-phase AC circuits that feed socket-outlets up to 32 A, and is described as required in higher-risk residential buildings, houses in multiple occupation, student accommodation and care homes. The exact wording is still being checked. Key rule: An AFDD detects dangerous arcing; it is recommended on single-phase socket-outlet circuits up to 32 A.

The supply's earthing arrangement decides how a fault is cleared. TN-S: the supplier provides a separate earth. TN-C-S (also called PME): the supplier combines neutral and earth, so the installation's earth comes from the neutral. TT: the installation uses its own earth electrode, so RCD protection is needed to clear faults, and the electrode resistance multiplied by the RCD trip current must stay at or below 50 V. The earthing conductor runs from the main earthing terminal to the electrode or the supplier's earth terminal, and is sized and protected against corrosion and mechanical damage. Key rule: Know TN-S, TN-C-S and TT: the arrangement decides how a fault clears and what protection is needed.

Extraneous metal that enters the building, such as gas and water service pipes and structural steel, is bonded to the main earthing terminal so that touch voltages stay low if a fault occurs. The size of the main bonding conductor follows from the supply neutral or earthing conductor: usually at least 6 mm² of copper and at most 25 mm², with 10 mm² common on PME supplies. In a room with a bath or shower, extra bonding can be left out only if all circuits there have RCD protection and automatic disconnection, and all incoming metal is already main-bonded. The circuit protective conductor is sized by the adiabatic equation or from a simplified table. Key rule: Bond incoming metal pipes and steel to the main earthing terminal, and size the bonding conductor from the supply conductor.

The protective device rating must sit between the circuit's design current and the cable's current-carrying capacity (Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz), and the device's guaranteed tripping current must not exceed 1.45 times the cable capacity. The device must also clear a short circuit before the cable overheats: the cable's heat-withstand limit must be higher than the let-through energy of the device. Key rule: Design current, then device rating, then cable capacity, in that order; and clear a short circuit before the cable overheats.

A cable's current-carrying capacity depends on how it is installed, the ambient temperature, grouping with other circuits and thermal insulation. Voltage drop from the origin of the installation to the load must stay within limits, commonly 3 percent for lighting and 5 percent for other circuits on a 230 V public supply. Key rule: Capacity depends on installation, temperature, grouping and insulation; keep voltage drop to about 3 percent for lighting and 5 percent otherwise.

The installation is divided into several circuits so that a fault affects as little as possible, safe maintenance is possible and nuisance tripping is limited. There is no fixed list of dedicated circuits. Key rule: Divide the installation so a fault affects as little as possible and maintenance is safe.

The designer assesses the maximum demand, with diversity, to size the supply and the conductors. The standard diversity tables are in industry guidance, not in the regulations themselves. Key rule: Assess the maximum demand, with diversity, before sizing the supply and conductors.

Every installation can be isolated by a main switch at its origin that opens all live conductors, and each circuit or item of equipment has isolation and switching suited to its use. The main switch must be accessible, and isolators can be secured against being switched on by mistake. Key rule: A main switch at the origin opens all live conductors and is accessible; isolators can be secured off.

A durable, legible chart, diagram or schedule at each consumer unit or distribution board shows the type and make-up of every circuit. In homes, the schedule from the electrical certificate fixed at the board usually meets this. A notice at the consumer unit tells users to press the RCD test button every six months. Single-phase installations use brown for the line, blue for the neutral and green-and-yellow for the circuit protective conductor; three-phase installations use brown, black and grey for the lines. Key rule: Label every circuit at the board, fit the RCD test notice, and use brown, blue and green-and-yellow correctly.

A cable concealed less than 50 mm below a wall surface must run in a safe zone (vertical and horizontal runs tied to accessories and corners) and have 30 mA RCD protection, unless it has another protection. A concealed cable can avoid the RCD requirement if it has an earthed metal sheath or earthed conduit or trunking, is protected against nails and screws by its construction or an earthed barrier, or is a SELV or PELV circuit. Key rule: A cable less than 50 mm deep in a wall runs in a safe zone with 30 mA RCD protection, unless it has one of the listed alternatives.

A room with a bath or shower is divided into zones. Zone 0 is inside the bath or shower tray, zone 1 is above it up to 2.25 m, and zone 2 extends 0.6 m beyond zone 1. Only very low voltage (SELV) equipment is allowed in zone 0, socket-outlets other than shaver units are not allowed in zones 0 to 2, and IP ratings and RCD protection apply across the zones. A swimming pool has zones 0, 1 and 2 too: zone 0 is the basin, where only SELV equipment is allowed, and metal parts such as ladders and rails are connected together by a supplementary bonding conductor. Each electric vehicle charging point needs 30 mA RCD protection plus protection against residual direct current. The exact wording for charging points is still being checked. Key rule: Zones decide what may go where in bathrooms and pools; charging points need an RCD and direct-current protection.

Equipment is installed so that it can be reached for operating, inspecting, testing and maintaining. There are no fixed clearance dimensions in the regulations; a duty to provide adequate working space comes from separate law. Key rule: Install equipment so it can be reached for operating, inspecting, testing and maintaining.

In homes, consumer units and similar boards are either made of non-combustible material (steel counts) or housed in a non-combustible cabinet. Installation work is carried out by competent people with proper materials, and connections are secure, suitable for the conductor and accessible for inspection. Key rule: Use a non-combustible consumer unit, competent workers and secure connections that can be inspected.

Title or circuit: Receptacles near sinks and wet areas
What it says: A standard 15 A or 20 A receptacle within 1.5 m of a sink, bathtub or shower stall, or outdoors within 2.5 m of the ground, needs Class A GFCI protection, which trips at a ground-fault current of 6 mA or more and never below 4 mA. The exception is a receptacle behind a fixed appliance, such as a clothes washer, that portable appliances cannot reach. Key rule: Standard receptacles within 1.5 m of water, or outdoors near the ground, need Class A GFCI protection.

Branch circuits that supply 125 V receptacles rated 20 A or less in a dwelling need combination-type AFCI protection. Some locations are exempt: refrigerator receptacles, kitchen counter, island and peninsula receptacles, and bathroom receptacles within 1 m of the wash basin. Key rule: Dwelling circuits for 125 V receptacles of 20 A or less need combination-type AFCI protection, with a short list of exemptions.

The code names what can serve as a grounding electrode. A manufactured electrode is normally two rods, each 3 m long, driven in full length, spaced at least 3 m apart and bonded together. Whether a buried metal water pipe may serve as an electrode depends on the province. All the grounding electrodes at a building are connected together so that they act as one grounding system. Metal piping and other non-electrical equipment that could become energized, including the building's metal water piping, are bonded to the grounding system with a bonding conductor. Key rule: Connect every grounding electrode into one system, and bond metal water piping to it.

An overcurrent device generally cannot be rated above the ampacity of the conductors it protects. For copper conductors the maximum device rating is 15 A for 14 AWG, 20 A for 12 AWG and 30 A for 10 AWG. A few small cords and wires have their own exceptions. Key rule: The device rating cannot exceed the conductor's ampacity: 15 A on 14 AWG, 20 A on 12 AWG, 30 A on 10 AWG.

Place dwelling-unit receptacles in finished walls so that every spot along the floor line of usable wall space (an unbroken run of 900 mm or more) is within 1.8 m of one, which makes 3.6 m the practical maximum gap between two receptacles. Behind kitchen counter work surfaces, install split receptacles so that you are never farther than 900 mm along the wall line from one. Sinks, built-in equipment and isolated work surfaces shorter than 300 mm at the wall line do not count. Key rule: No point on usable wall is more than 1.8 m from a receptacle, and none on a kitchen counter more than 900 mm.

Leave at least 1 m of clear working space about electrical equipment wherever it must be reached for operation or maintenance: the front and, where access is needed there, the sides or back, plus any extra room that draw-out devices such as breakers or starters need when fully withdrawn. In a dwelling unit, mount no branch-circuit breaker or switch with its handle more than 1.7 m above the finished floor. The main is excepted. Key rule: Keep at least 1 m clear around equipment, and keep dwelling breaker handles no higher than 1.7 m.

Put the consumer's service equipment where it is readily accessible and close to where the service conductors enter the building. It does not belong in places such as clothes closets, bathrooms, stairways or spaces with low headroom. A motor's disconnecting means is installed in sight of the motor and its starter, and within 9 m of them. Key rule: Service equipment is readily accessible near where the supply enters; a motor's disconnect is in sight and within 9 m.

Ground-Fault Circuit Interrupter (GFCI) protection is required for 125 V to 250 V receptacles in a dwelling's bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, basements, laundry areas, within 6 ft of sinks, and near bathtubs and showers, and for the outlets that supply dishwashers. Key rule: 125 V to 250 V receptacles in these dwelling locations need GFCI protection.

Arc-Fault Circuit Interrupter (AFCI) protection is required for 120 V, 15 A and 20 A branch circuits that serve the dwelling-unit rooms the code lists: bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens, dining rooms, hallways, closets, laundry areas and similar rooms. Key rule: AFCI protection is required in the listed habitable rooms of dwelling units.

Wire gauge must match the breaker amperage: 14 AWG max 15A, 12 AWG max 20A, 10 AWG max 30A, 8 AWG max 40A, 6 AWG max 55A. Never put a smaller wire on a larger breaker. Key rule: 14 AWG = 15A, 12 AWG = 20A, 10 AWG = 30A, 8 AWG = 40A, 6 AWG = 55A

Dwelling units need 20 A circuits for the bathroom receptacles and the laundry receptacle, and at least two 20 A small-appliance circuits for the kitchen countertop and nearby eating areas. Key rule: Bathroom, laundry, and kitchen small-appliance circuits are 20 A circuits of their own.

Wall receptacles: no point more than 6 feet from an outlet (max 12 feet between outlets). Countertop receptacles: no point more than 24 inches from an outlet. Islands and peninsulas 24"x12" or larger need at least one outlet. Key rule: Walls: 6ft rule (12ft max spacing). Countertops: 24-inch rule.

Standard method: General lighting at 3 VA/sq ft + small-appliance circuits at 1,500 VA each + laundry at 1,500 VA. Apply the standard demand factors: first 3,000 VA at 100%, remainder at 35%. Add dryer (5,000 VA) and range (8,000 VA demand) at 100%. Key rule: 3 VA/sq ft lighting + 1,500 VA per SA circuit + standard demand factors

All grounding electrodes present at a building must be bonded together. Common electrodes: metal underground water pipe (10ft+ contact), ground rods (8ft, 5/8" diameter), concrete-encased electrode (Ufer ground). The grounding electrode conductor connects the system to earth. Key rule: All present electrodes must be bonded together to form the grounding electrode system.

Panelboards must not exceed their bus rating. All circuits must be identified in a directory. Working space: 30" wide, 36" deep, 6.5' high minimum. Balance loads between bus sides. Main breaker must handle the calculated service load. Key rule: Panel directory required. Do not exceed bus rating. Maintain working clearance.

NM (Romex) cable must be secured within 12 inches of every box and at intervals not exceeding 4.5 feet. When more than 2 NM cables pass through the same hole in framing that is sealed with insulation, caulk or foam, ampacity must be derated using the code's adjustment factors. Key rule: Secure within 12" of boxes, every 4.5 ft. Derate when bundling 3+ cables in a sealed opening.

Keep clear, usable space around panels and other equipment that is worked on live. The space in front is as deep as the code's table gives, at least 30 inches wide (or as wide as the equipment if that is more), and clear from the floor up to 6-1/2 ft or the top of the equipment if that is taller. The space above the panel, equal to its width and depth, is reserved for the electrical installation and holds no pipes or ducts. Breakers and switches must be within reach: the grip of the handle at its top position is no higher than 6 ft 7 in. Key rule: Keep the space in front of and above a panel clear, wide enough and high enough to work in, and keep the handles within reach.

Every supply needs a way to cut it off. The service disconnect is readily accessible, outside the building or inside near where the service conductors enter, and its rating is at least the calculated load. A service normally has one disconnect; up to six are permitted for each service. A building supplied by a feeder or branch circuit needs a means to disconnect all its ungrounded conductors. A fixed appliance over 300 VA may use its branch-circuit breaker as its disconnect only if the breaker is in sight of the appliance or can be locked open. Key rule: Know where each disconnect must be, how many are allowed, and what it must be rated for.

Marking tells the next person what they are touching. Every circuit, and every change to one, is labelled with its specific purpose in enough detail to tell it from the others; a label may not depend on who lives there. Each disconnecting means is marked with its purpose unless its place makes that obvious, and the service disconnect is marked as such. Grounded conductors of 6 AWG or smaller are white or gray (or striped), and equipment grounding conductors are green or green with a yellow stripe, which is never used for a circuit conductor. A switch or breaker shows clearly whether it is on or off. Key rule: Label circuits and disconnects clearly, and use the right insulation colors for grounded and grounding conductors.

Water changes what equipment is allowed. A receptacle outdoors under cover, or in another damp location, needs an enclosure that is weatherproof when its covers are closed. In a wet location the enclosure stays weatherproof with or without a plug in it, which in practice means an in-use cover. Luminaires in damp or wet locations are mounted so water cannot get into or collect in their wiring compartments or lampholders. Around a pool, other receptacles must be at least 6 ft from the inside wall, and the pool's conductive parts are bonded together with solid copper no smaller than 8 AWG. Key rule: Match the enclosure to how wet the place is, and keep receptacles and bonding right around pools.

A breaker or fuse protects the conductor, so its rating must match the conductor's ampacity. Breakers and fixed-trip fuses come in standard ratings, and where the ampacity falls between two, the next size up may be used, but not for a circuit with more than one receptacle for portable cord-and-plug loads. Small copper conductors have set limits: 14 AWG 15 A, 12 AWG 20 A, 10 AWG 30 A. No overcurrent device goes in series with an intentionally grounded conductor unless it opens every conductor of the circuit together. A panelboard is protected by a device rated no higher than the panelboard itself. Key rule: Size the breaker to the conductor, use standard ratings, and never put a device in the grounded conductor alone.

Equipment is installed and used the way its listing or labeling says, with good workmanship. Connectors and lugs must suit the conductor material. Conductors are terminated securely, without nicking or crushing them. Choose the conductor's temperature rating so it does not exceed the lowest rating among the connected terminations, conductors or devices. Internal parts such as busbars, terminals and insulators must not be damaged or contaminated by paint, plaster, cleaners or other foreign material. Key rule: Follow the listing, match the connector to the metal, terminate carefully, and keep to the lowest temperature rating.

Boxes and conduit bodies must be big enough for every conductor inside, and installed so the wiring is accessible. In a noncombustible finish the front edge of a flush box must not sit more than 1/4 in. behind the surface; in a combustible finish it must be flush or project. At each outlet leave at least 6 in. of free conductor, and at least 3 in. outside an opening under 8 in. Cable through holes in framing stays at least 1-1/4 in. from the wood's edge, or is shielded. NM cable bends need a radius of at least five times the cable diameter, and the cable is protected where it can be damaged. Key rule: Size and place boxes for the conductors and the finish, leave working length, and protect cable at framing and bends.

A panelboard goes in an enclosure made for it and is dead front, so no live parts can be touched from the operating side. Each cable entering is secured to the enclosure. Unused openings, including those meant for breakers, are closed so the protection is close to that of the enclosure wall. Each grounded conductor ends in its own terminal unless the terminal is marked for more than one, and a panelboard must prevent more overcurrent devices being installed than it is rated and listed for. Key rule: Keep the enclosure closed and dead front, secure each cable, and keep terminations and the device count within the panelboard's listing.

Key rule: 125 V to 250 V receptacles in these dwelling locations need GFCI protection.
